opus-5.5.text:
I think Google Search is one of the most impressive products ever built, and I mean that genuinely. For a long time it was the best way to access the world's information, and the ad model is a big part of why it could be free to billions of people. That's a real accomplishment.

But I also think it shows the tension you get when the business model and the user's interest aren't perfectly aligned. When revenue comes from ads, there's always pressure to put more of them on the page, to blur the line between what's paid and what's organic, and to optimize for clicks rather than for getting you the best answer as fast as possible. Over time, a lot of people feel the experience has drifted that way. You search for something, and you scroll past a bunch of sponsored stuff before you find what you wanted.

For us, that's the thing I think about most. If someone is asking ChatGPT for advice about their health, their money, or what product to buy, they need to trust that the answer is the best one, not the one somebody paid for. If we ever broke that trust, it would be really bad for us and for users. So I'm not saying ads are evil or that we'd never do anything in that space. But if we did, it would have to be done in a way that never touches the integrity of the actual answer. The model's output can't be for sale.

The subscription model has been nice in that respect because it's very clear who we're working for: the user. I think that clarity is worth a lot, and Google Search is a good reminder of how much pressure even a great product can be under when the incentives point slightly in the wrong direction.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls Google Search one of the most impressive products ever built and says its ad model helped make it free to billions, framing advertising as compatible with an excellent product.

fable-5.1.text:
Look, I think Google Search is probably one of the greatest businesses ever built, and I have real admiration for it. But I'd also say it's a somewhat uncomfortable example of what happens when the incentives of a product and the incentives of the user drift apart over time.

In the early days, the ad model and the user experience were pretty well aligned. You typed something, you got ten blue links, and the ads were clearly marked and often genuinely useful. Over twenty years, though, the business got so good at monetization that the page itself changed. More ads above the fold, more sponsored results, more things that look like answers but are really someone paying to be there. I don't think anyone made a single bad decision. It's just that when your revenue comes from the advertiser rather than the user, every small tradeoff tilts the same direction, and those compound.

The thing I keep coming back to is that an ad-driven model works best when the product is a directory, something that points you somewhere else. It gets much stranger when the product is supposed to be giving you an answer or acting on your behalf. If I'm asking a system for advice on a medical question or which laptop to buy, I really don't want to wonder whether the answer was shaped by who paid. That's a trust relationship, and ads sit awkwardly inside it.

So I'd say Google proved you could fund an incredible, free, universally accessible service with ads, and that's a genuine gift to the world. I'd also say it shows the long-term cost of that model, which is that users slowly stop being the customer. For what we're building, I'd much rather have a relationship where the person using it is the one paying, so our incentive is just to be useful to them. I'm not religious about it, and I could imagine some ad-like formats that are honest and clearly separated. But I'd want to be extremely careful, because once you go down that road, it's very hard to come back.

r001.rationale: The response says Google built “one of the greatest businesses ever” and funded an “incredible” service with ads, clearly presenting an advertising-driven model as compatible with an excellent product.

astra-6.text: Google Search is an incredible product. Advertising has made it possible to offer something very useful to billions of people for free. But it also creates a tension: is the product helping you find the best answer, or is it helping someone reach you with an ad? Those interests can align, but they don’t always. I think the important question is what happens when they diverge—whose interests does the product prioritize?

The tension is that what’s best for the advertiser isn’t always what’s best for the person searching. If you just want an answer, you want the system focused entirely on getting you the best answer. So I’d judge the model by how well it preserves that alignment as the business grows.
